transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, thanks. Um… the main thing is work, honestly. I’m a nurse, and on the floor I keep losing my train of thought in ways that are starting to feel really unmanageable. Like I’ll be in the middle of thinking through a patient flow issue—who needs to be moved, what needs to happen next, what I was about to follow up on—and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone near me asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and it’s like my brain just drops the thread completely.

And I know those interruptions are part of the job, I do, but it’s the way I can’t get back to what I was doing. I’ll stand there for a second trying to retrace my steps, like, “What was I just solving?” and sometimes it’s just gone. It’s really frustrating and honestly kind of scary because the floor is already busy, and I feel like I’m constantly getting pulled off track by every sound or question around me.
Did you have problems with focus or distractibility like this when you were a child?

Yeah… looking back, yes. I mean, I didn’t think of it that way at the time because I was always told I was “bright,” so it got framed more like I was careless or not trying hard enough. But even in elementary school, my teachers would write things on report cards like, “She’s very capable, but she loses worksheets,” or “forgets to turn in homework,” or makes careless mistakes.

And my mom really had to sit with me every night to get homework done. Not because I couldn’t understand it — I usually could — but because I’d drift off, or forget what I was supposed to be doing, or somehow the worksheet would disappear between school and home. She’d basically keep redirecting me step by step, like, “Okay, finish this part, now put it in your folder, now put the folder in your backpack,” because if she didn’t, I’d go to school without it or it just wouldn’t get turned in. So… yes, it’s been there for a long time, it just looked more like being disorganized or careless when I was little.
Do these same focus problems happen outside of work too?

Yes, definitely. It’s not just at work, although work is where it feels the most high-stakes. At home it’s this constant thing where I forget things that should be routine, and then I feel ridiculous because I really did mean to do them.

Like I’ll tell myself, “I need to call my sister back after dinner,” and then suddenly it’s two days later and I’m seeing her missed call again like, oh my God, I never called her. Or I’ll have a bill that I know needs to be paid, and I’ll even put a reminder in my phone sometimes, but if I don’t do it right that second, it’s like it disappears from my brain again. Same with appointments — I’ve missed things or almost missed things even when I had every intention of going.

And it happens with practical things too, not just personal stuff. Like if there’s something I need to follow up on, even outside the immediate chaos of the floor, it can just fall out of my head. I’ll remember later and feel awful because it wasn’t that I didn’t care. I did care. I just… didn’t hold onto it somehow. It makes me feel unreliable, which is really upsetting because I’m trying so hard not to be.
When something is really interesting to you, do you sometimes get so absorbed in it that you lose track of time?

Um… I’m not totally sure, actually. I mean, I know people talk about getting “lost” in something when they really like it, but I don’t know if I’ve noticed that as a clear pattern for me.

Sometimes if something is genuinely interesting, I can stay with it better than if it’s boring, obviously, but I don’t know that I’d say I regularly lose hours or forget the world exists. Or maybe I do sometimes and I just haven’t really paid attention to it that way. I guess I’d have to think about specific examples.

So… I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I think it’s possible, but it’s not one of the main things I’ve been noticing or worrying about.
When you’re losing your train of thought, are you also feeling anxious in that moment?

I’m not sure. Sometimes I think I get anxious after I notice I’ve lost it, if that makes sense — like I’m talking and then suddenly I realize I don’t know where I was going, and then I feel embarrassed or pressured to recover it quickly.

But I don’t know that anxiety is always there first. A lot of the time it just feels like my thought kind of slips away, and then the anxiety comes in because I’m aware it happened, especially if someone is waiting for me to finish what I was saying. So… I’m not totally sure how to separate those two in the moment.
Have you been feeling depressed most days?

I don’t think so… not “depressed most days,” at least not in the way I understand that. I mean, I definitely get frustrated with myself and upset when I keep dropping the ball or when I feel like I’m not functioning the way I should, and that can make me feel pretty low in the moment.

But if you mean like a persistent depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, I don’t know that I’d say that’s been the main thing. I haven’t really been tracking my mood that way, honestly. I guess I feel overwhelmed and discouraged a lot, but I’m not sure I would call it depression most days.
Did these concentration problems get noticeably worse after a major stressful event in your life?

I don’t know if I’d describe it as after a major stressful event exactly, like one sudden thing happened and then everything changed overnight. But it did become a major problem after I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities, almost two years ago now.

Before that, I mean, I’m sure I had moments where I was scattered or had trouble focusing, but it became much more noticeable when my role got bigger. There were just more moving pieces to keep track of, more responsibility, and more interruptions, and that’s when I started really feeling like my concentration wasn’t keeping up with what was expected of me.

So… if that counts as a stressful change, then yes, that’s around when it got noticeably worse. Not one big dramatic event, but that shift in responsibilities was definitely the point where it became a major issue.
Aside from work, have these focus problems caused significant problems in other parts of your life?

Honestly, the biggest and most obvious problems have been at work. I know you asked aside from work, but that’s where it’s gotten severe enough that it’s hard for me not to go there first.

It’s not just that I feel scattered or annoyed with myself — it’s gotten to the point where I’m on formal supervision, and other nurses are having to double-check parts of my follow-through when I’m functioning as charge. That feels awful, because I’m supposed to be the person coordinating things and keeping track, and instead I feel like people are watching to make sure I didn’t miss something.

It makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader, which is really painful to say out loud. I don’t want to be someone my coworkers have to compensate for. So, in terms of “significant problems,” yes — at least at work, absolutely. Outside of work, I’d have to think more carefully, but the work impairment is the one that feels really serious and concrete.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I worry, definitely, but I don’t know if I’d call it excessive worrying about many different things for no reason. A lot of what I worry about feels tied to something specific, like whether I’ve missed something or whether I’m going to fall behind, so it doesn’t feel like this free-floating worry about everything.

If there isn’t an immediate problem to solve, I don’t think I’m usually sitting there worrying about a whole list of unrelated things. At least… not that I’ve noticed in that way. I can get stuck thinking about things, but I’m not sure if that’s the kind of worry you mean.
Outside of work, have these attention problems caused serious problems in your daily life?

Yes… I think they have. Not always in the same dramatic way as work, but when I really look at it, it does spill over into daily life more than I like to admit.

I forget things that should be routine — like calling a family member back. I’ll fully intend to do it, and I’ll even think, “Okay, I need to call them tonight,” and then somehow it’s just gone from my mind until days later when I feel awful. Or I’ll miss following up on something that I know I needed to check on, like a missing order or some loose end, and it’s not because I didn’t care. It’s like it doesn’t stay in the front of my brain long enough.

At home it happens with bills too, which is embarrassing because I’m not trying to be irresponsible. I’ll see the bill, make a mental note, sometimes even set a reminder, and then either dismiss the reminder because I’m in the middle of something or I think I’ll do it “in a minute,” and then I just don’t. Same with appointments — I’ve had times where I meant to go, I knew about it, and then the day gets away from me or I remember too late.

So yes, outside work it has caused real problems. It’s not just being a little forgetful. It’s forgetting things that normal adults are supposed to be able to keep track of, even when I’m trying to put systems in place, and that’s been really frustrating and honestly kind of humiliating.
Do you often feel restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?

I don’t think so… not in the sense of feeling physically restless all the time or like I can’t stay in a chair. I mean, I can sit through things if I need to. I don’t usually feel like I’m crawling out of my skin or needing to pace around constantly.

Sometimes I might shift around or get up if I’m uncomfortable or if I’ve been sitting a long time, but I don’t think that’s a major issue for me. It’s not something people have really commented on, and it’s not the thing I would point to as a problem. For me, if I’m struggling, it’s usually not because my body won’t stay still — it’s more that… well, I guess I’m not sure how to put it without getting into other stuff. But no, the restless, hard-to-sit-still part doesn’t really sound like me.
When you lose your train of thought, is it usually because another thought in your mind pulls you away?

Yes, that happens a lot. I think that’s actually one of the main reasons I’m here, honestly.

On the floor, I’ll be in the middle of thinking through something — like a patient flow issue, or what needs to happen next for one patient, or who needs what first — and then some other stimulus or thought just yanks me away. An IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, and suddenly the thing I was holding in my head is just… gone. Not always gone forever, but gone enough that I have to stop and retrace what I was doing.

It’s not always even that the new thing is more important. It just grabs my attention before I can decide whether it should. Like I’ll hear a pump alarm and my brain turns toward that, and then by the time I come back, I’ve forgotten what patient flow problem I was trying to solve or what step I was about to take. It makes me feel scattered, and it’s really frustrating because in my job there are interruptions constantly, so I feel like I’m getting pulled off course over and over again.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on a task or conversation all the way through, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because it depends what you mean by “all the way through.” Like… I don’t know if I’d say I’m consciously noticing, “I can’t focus right now,” every time it happens.

If I’m really trying, I can sometimes stay with something, especially if it’s important or if someone is directly in front of me. But I guess I’d have to think more about whether I’m actually focused the whole time or whether I’m sort of forcing myself back to it repeatedly. I don’t know if that distinction matters.

So… I’m not trying to dodge the question. I just don’t know that I’ve paid attention to it in that exact way. I can tell you that staying mentally “locked in” doesn’t always feel easy, but I’m not sure how often it happens or how to measure it.
Do you often start reading something and realize a few minutes later that you haven’t really taken in what you just read?

I’m not sure. I mean… I know what you mean, like reading a page and then realizing none of it actually went in. I don’t know if I’ve tracked how often that happens to me.

I don’t do a ton of reading for fun lately, so maybe it’s harder for me to judge. If I’m reading something important, I might reread parts, but I don’t always know whether that’s because I didn’t absorb it or just because I want to make sure I understood it correctly. Like with instructions or something work-related, I tend to be careful anyway, so I may go back over it.

So… I guess my honest answer is I’m not really sure. It probably happens sometimes, because I think that happens to everyone, but I don’t know that I can say “often” with confidence.
In meetings or conversations, do you often realize your mind has drifted and you missed part of what was being said?

Yes — I mean, especially at work, absolutely. That’s kind of the big thing I keep circling back to, because it feels like my attention gets pulled away before I even realize it’s happening.

Like on the floor, I’ll be thinking through a patient flow issue or trying to keep track of what needs to happen next, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and my brain just switches over to that. Then when I come back, I’ll realize I missed whatever I was supposed to be tracking in my own head, or I’ll have lost the thread of what someone was saying.

It’s not always that I’m bored or not trying to listen. That’s the frustrating part. I can be trying to pay attention, but there are so many little interruptions, and they hook me so fast. Then I’m standing there like, “Wait, what was I doing?” or “What did they just say?” and I have to mentally backtrack. It happens constantly enough that it’s one of the main reasons I came in.
When you’re off duty and there’s nothing urgent to handle, do you still find it hard to relax because your mind keeps going?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t know that I’ve paid close enough attention to what my mind does when I’m off duty in that specific way.

I mean, when I get home, sometimes I’m tired enough that I don’t really know if my mind is “racing” or if I’m just kind of decompressing and thinking through random things. And I don’t always know what counts as hard to relax. Like, if I’m sitting there and I’m not fully settled, is that my mind keeping going, or is that just normal after a shift? I’m not sure.

I wouldn’t want to say yes just because it sounds like something that could fit. I’d have to think about it more. I know work can leave me feeling keyed up sometimes, but whether that’s happening when there’s nothing urgent and whether it’s enough that I can’t relax… I don’t really have a clear answer.
When you’re in a quiet place with no interruptions, do you still lose track of what you’re doing?

I think it’s much more obvious when there are interruptions. Like, the main reason I’m here is what happens on the floor — I’ll be trying to hold a patient flow issue in my head, or remember what I was about to do next, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something nearby, or a call light goes off, and suddenly the whole thing is just gone. I’ll be standing there trying to reconstruct what I was doing.

If I’m in a quiet place with no interruptions, it’s harder for me to answer as clearly. I don’t want to say it never happens, but it’s not the example that jumps out at me. The pattern I notice most is that my train of thought gets knocked off track so easily by anything around me. It’s like I’m fine for a second, and then one small thing pulls my attention, and I lose the thread of what I was working on.
When there isn’t noise or interruption around you, do you still find your mind drifting off the task?

I guess that’s the part I’m having a harder time separating out. When there isn’t noise or interruption, I don’t notice it in the same dramatic way, if that makes sense.

The reason I keep coming back to work is because that’s where it’s so obvious and constant. On the floor, I’ll be holding some patient flow issue in my head — like what needs to happen next, who I need to check on, or what step I was about to take — and then an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and it’s like my train of thought just disappears. Suddenly I’ve forgotten what I was working on, and I’m standing there trying to rewind the last few seconds and figure out where I left off.

So if I’m in a quiet room with nothing pulling at me, I’m not sure I’d describe it the same way. Maybe my mind still wanders some, but the main issue I’m really aware of is how easily even small things around me knock me off track. That’s the thing that’s been causing problems and making me feel like I can’t keep my thoughts together when I need to.
Do you often feel unable to control your worrying?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that one. I don’t know that I would describe what happens to me as “worrying” exactly, or at least I haven’t really tracked it that way.

Like, I can get caught up thinking about things, and sometimes I’ll go over stuff in my head, but when you say “unable to control worrying,” I’m not sure if you mean feeling anxious and unable to stop, or more like mentally replaying things, or just having thoughts that keep coming back. Those feel a little different to me, and I don’t want to say yes if I’m just interpreting it wrong.

I guess I haven’t noticed a clear pattern of, like, sitting there worrying and feeling like I absolutely can’t shut it off. It may happen sometimes, but it’s not something I’ve specifically identified as a major issue. I’d probably need an example of what you mean to answer more accurately.
When you're doing something routine at home in a quiet setting, do you still find your mind drifting off what you're doing?

At home, if it’s quiet and I’m doing something routine, I’m honestly less sure. I don’t notice it as clearly there, or at least it doesn’t stand out to me in the same way.

The thing that made me come in is really what happens at work. On the floor, I’ll be trying to keep a patient flow issue in my head — like what I was about to do next, or who needed what, or what step I was in the middle of — and then something small happens around me. An IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question nearby, a call light goes off, and suddenly it’s like the thought just drops out of my head. I’ll be standing there thinking, “Wait, what was I just doing?” and trying to piece it back together.

So with a quiet routine thing at home, I don’t want to overstate it. Maybe it happens some, but it’s not the pattern I’m most aware of. What feels constant and really disruptive is how easily I lose my train of thought when something pulls my attention, especially on the floor.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive, generalized worry or anxiety across many topics, which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I worry, definitely, but I don’t know if I’d call it excessive worrying about many different things for no reason. A lot of what I worry about feels tied to something specific, like whether I’ve missed something or whether I’m going to fall behind, so it doesn’t feel like this free-floating worry about everything.

If there isn’t an immediate problem to solve, I don’t think I’m usually sitting there worrying about a whole list of unrelated things. At least… not that I’ve noticed in that way. I can get stuck thinking about things, but I’m not sure if that’s the kind of worry you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems occur across multiple settings with clear non-work impairment, which would help distinguish ADHD from context-specific stress or anxiety-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Outside of work, have these attention problems caused serious problems in your daily life?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I forget things that should be routine, like calling a family member back, following up on a missing order, paying a bill at home, or showing up for an appointment, even when I meant to do it and sometimes even after I set a reminder.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about attention-related problems outside of work in everyday life, which is best captured by forgetfulness in daily activities like returning calls, paying bills, and keeping appointments.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think they have. Not always in the same dramatic way as work, but when I really look at it, it does spill over into daily life more than I like to admit.

I forget things that should be routine — like calling a family member back. I’ll fully intend to do it, and I’ll even think, “Okay, I need to call them tonight,” and then somehow it’s just gone from my mind until days later when I feel awful. Or I’ll miss following up on something that I know I needed to check on, like a missing order or some loose end, and it’s not because I didn’t care. It’s like it doesn’t stay in the front of my brain long enough.

At home it happens with bills too, which is embarrassing because I’m not trying to be irresponsible. I’ll see the bill, make a mental note, sometimes even set a reminder, and then either dismiss the reminder because I’m in the middle of something or I think I’ll do it “in a minute,” and then I just don’t. Same with appointments — I’ve had times where I meant to go, I knew about it, and then the day gets away from me or I remember too late.

So yes, outside work it has caused real problems. It’s not just being a little forgetful. It’s forgetting things that normal adults are supposed to be able to keep track of, even when I’m trying to put systems in place, and that’s been really frustrating and honestly kind of humiliating.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is significant hyperactivity/impulsivity, which would help distinguish ADHD predominantly inattentive type from nonspecific concentration problems related to anxiety, stress, or depression.
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?

target_item.reason: The question is about restlessness or difficulty sitting still, which is a hyperactivity symptom not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the sense of feeling physically restless all the time or like I can’t stay in a chair. I mean, I can sit through things if I need to. I don’t usually feel like I’m crawling out of my skin or needing to pace around constantly.

Sometimes I might shift around or get up if I’m uncomfortable or if I’ve been sitting a long time, but I don’t think that’s a major issue for me. It’s not something people have really commented on, and it’s not the thing I would point to as a problem. For me, if I’m struggling, it’s usually not because my body won’t stay still — it’s more that… well, I guess I’m not sure how to put it without getting into other stuff. But no, the restless, hard-to-sit-still part doesn’t really sound like me.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the attentional lapses are due to internal distractibility/racing thoughts, which helps distinguish ADHD from anxiety or stress-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: When you lose your train of thought, is it usually because another thought in your mind pulls you away?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether losing the train of thought is due to being pulled away by another internal thought, which directly matches distractibility, including unrelated thoughts.

patient.answer:
Yes, that happens a lot. I think that’s actually one of the main reasons I’m here, honestly.

On the floor, I’ll be in the middle of thinking through something — like a patient flow issue, or what needs to happen next for one patient, or who needs what first — and then some other stimulus or thought just yanks me away. An IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, and suddenly the thing I was holding in my head is just… gone. Not always gone forever, but gone enough that I have to stop and retrace what I was doing.

It’s not always even that the new thing is more important. It just grabs my attention before I can decide whether it should. Like I’ll hear a pump alarm and my brain turns toward that, and then by the time I come back, I’ve forgotten what patient flow problem I was trying to solve or what step I was about to take. It makes me feel scattered, and it’s really frustrating because in my job there are interruptions constantly, so I feel like I’m getting pulled off course over and over again.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD inattentive type from a primary concentration complaint by testing for another core inattentive symptom: difficulty sustaining attention during tasks or conversations.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble staying focused on a task or conversation all the way through, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or conversations, but the provided symptom profile does not include a sustained-attention item. The closest listed item is distractibility, but that is specifically about being pulled away by external stimuli or unrelated thoughts, so I should not force it.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because it depends what you mean by “all the way through.” Like… I don’t know if I’d say I’m consciously noticing, “I can’t focus right now,” every time it happens.

If I’m really trying, I can sometimes stay with something, especially if it’s important or if someone is directly in front of me. But I guess I’d have to think more about whether I’m actually focused the whole time or whether I’m sort of forcing myself back to it repeatedly. I don’t know if that distinction matters.

So… I’m not trying to dodge the question. I just don’t know that I’ve paid attention to it in that exact way. I can tell you that staying mentally “locked in” doesn’t always feel easy, but I’m not sure how often it happens or how to measure it.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the attention problem includes poor sustained attention, a core inattentive ADHD symptom that helps distinguish ADHD from stress-, anxiety-, or mood-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Do you often start reading something and realize a few minutes later that you haven’t really taken in what you just read?

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about difficulty sustaining attention while reading, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific sustained-attention item. The available items cover distractibility, organization, avoidance of sustained effort, mistakes, forgetfulness, and other areas, but not this exact reading-focused sustained attention problem.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean… I know what you mean, like reading a page and then realizing none of it actually went in. I don’t know if I’ve tracked how often that happens to me.

I don’t do a ton of reading for fun lately, so maybe it’s harder for me to judge. If I’m reading something important, I might reread parts, but I don’t always know whether that’s because I didn’t absorb it or just because I want to make sure I understood it correctly. Like with instructions or something work-related, I tend to be careful anyway, so I may go back over it.

So… I guess my honest answer is I’m not really sure. It probably happens sometimes, because I think that happens to everyone, but I don’t know that I can say “often” with confidence.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the attention problems involve persistent difficulty sustaining attention, which would help distinguish ADHD inattentive type from nonspecific concentration problems related to anxiety, stress, or depression.
doctor.question: In meetings or conversations, do you often realize your mind has drifted and you missed part of what was being said?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mind drifting during meetings or conversations and missing what was said, which is most directly about being distracted by unrelated thoughts or stimuli.

patient.answer:
Yes — I mean, especially at work, absolutely. That’s kind of the big thing I keep circling back to, because it feels like my attention gets pulled away before I even realize it’s happening.

Like on the floor, I’ll be thinking through a patient flow issue or trying to keep track of what needs to happen next, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and my brain just switches over to that. Then when I come back, I’ll realize I missed whatever I was supposed to be tracking in my own head, or I’ll have lost the thread of what someone was saying.

It’s not always that I’m bored or not trying to listen. That’s the frustrating part. I can be trying to pay attention, but there are so many little interruptions, and they hook me so fast. Then I’m standing there like, “Wait, what was I doing?” or “What did they just say?” and I have to mentally backtrack. It happens constantly enough that it’s one of the main reasons I came in.

doctor.intent: Differentiate primary ADHD from concentration problems better explained by anxiety by testing for difficulty relaxing during non-demand periods.
doctor.question: When you’re off duty and there’s nothing urgent to handle, do you still find it hard to relax because your mind keeps going?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty relaxing or an overactive/racing mind when off duty, which is not directly covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t know that I’ve paid close enough attention to what my mind does when I’m off duty in that specific way.

I mean, when I get home, sometimes I’m tired enough that I don’t really know if my mind is “racing” or if I’m just kind of decompressing and thinking through random things. And I don’t always know what counts as hard to relax. Like, if I’m sitting there and I’m not fully settled, is that my mind keeping going, or is that just normal after a shift? I’m not sure.

I wouldn’t want to say yes just because it sounds like something that could fit. I’d have to think about it more. I know work can leave me feeling keyed up sometimes, but whether that’s happening when there’s nothing urgent and whether it’s enough that I can’t relax… I don’t really have a clear answer.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the attention problems are limited to distractibility in stimulating environments versus a broader sustained-attention deficit, to better distinguish ADHD from nonspecific concentration problems related to anxiety, stress, or depression.
doctor.question: When you’re in a quiet place with no interruptions, do you still lose track of what you’re doing?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether attention is lost even without external interruptions, which is closest to losing track of what one is doing due to distractibility, including unrelated thoughts.

patient.answer:
I think it’s much more obvious when there are interruptions. Like, the main reason I’m here is what happens on the floor — I’ll be trying to hold a patient flow issue in my head, or remember what I was about to do next, and then an IV pump beeps, or someone asks another nurse something nearby, or a call light goes off, and suddenly the whole thing is just gone. I’ll be standing there trying to reconstruct what I was doing.

If I’m in a quiet place with no interruptions, it’s harder for me to answer as clearly. I don’t want to say it never happens, but it’s not the example that jumps out at me. The pattern I notice most is that my train of thought gets knocked off track so easily by anything around me. It’s like I’m fine for a second, and then one small thing pulls my attention, and I lose the thread of what I was working on.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD from anxiety/stress-related concentration problems by testing whether attentional lapses occur even without external distractions.
doctor.question: When there isn’t noise or interruption around you, do you still find your mind drifting off the task?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether attention drifts off-task even without external noise or interruptions, which is most directly about distractibility/losing train of thought rather than organization, forgetfulness, or task avoidance.

patient.answer:
I guess that’s the part I’m having a harder time separating out. When there isn’t noise or interruption, I don’t notice it in the same dramatic way, if that makes sense.

The reason I keep coming back to work is because that’s where it’s so obvious and constant. On the floor, I’ll be holding some patient flow issue in my head — like what needs to happen next, who I need to check on, or what step I was about to take — and then an IV pump beeps, or someone nearby asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and it’s like my train of thought just disappears. Suddenly I’ve forgotten what I was working on, and I’m standing there trying to rewind the last few seconds and figure out where I left off.

So if I’m in a quiet room with nothing pulling at me, I’m not sure I’d describe it the same way. Maybe my mind still wanders some, but the main issue I’m really aware of is how easily even small things around me knock me off track. That’s the thing that’s been causing problems and making me feel like I can’t keep my thoughts together when I need to.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is a sustained, generalized anxiety pattern driving the concentration problems, helping distinguish ADHD from an anxiety disorder or stress-related condition.
doctor.question: Do you often feel unable to control your worrying?

target_item.reason: The question is about uncontrollable worrying/anxiety, which is not covered by the listed ADHD inattentive or related symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that one. I don’t know that I would describe what happens to me as “worrying” exactly, or at least I haven’t really tracked it that way.

Like, I can get caught up thinking about things, and sometimes I’ll go over stuff in my head, but when you say “unable to control worrying,” I’m not sure if you mean feeling anxious and unable to stop, or more like mentally replaying things, or just having thoughts that keep coming back. Those feel a little different to me, and I don’t want to say yes if I’m just interpreting it wrong.

I guess I haven’t noticed a clear pattern of, like, sitting there worrying and feeling like I absolutely can’t shut it off. It may happen sometimes, but it’s not something I’ve specifically identified as a major issue. I’d probably need an example of what you mean to answer more accurately.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problem persists without external distraction, which helps distinguish ADHD/inattentiveness from distraction mainly driven by a high-interruption work setting or stress.
doctor.question: When you're doing something routine at home in a quiet setting, do you still find your mind drifting off what you're doing?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether attention drifts away from the task even in a quiet, routine home setting, which most directly relates to distractibility, including distraction by unrelated thoughts.

patient.answer:
At home, if it’s quiet and I’m doing something routine, I’m honestly less sure. I don’t notice it as clearly there, or at least it doesn’t stand out to me in the same way.

The thing that made me come in is really what happens at work. On the floor, I’ll be trying to keep a patient flow issue in my head — like what I was about to do next, or who needed what, or what step I was in the middle of — and then something small happens around me. An IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question nearby, a call light goes off, and suddenly it’s like the thought just drops out of my head. I’ll be standing there thinking, “Wait, what was I just doing?” and trying to piece it back together.

So with a quiet routine thing at home, I don’t want to overstate it. Maybe it happens some, but it’s not the pattern I’m most aware of. What feels constant and really disruptive is how easily I lose my train of thought when something pulls my attention, especially on the floor.
